analysis.one_liner: Bars dumping mining and other waste into rivers and streams under the looser 'fill' permit process.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 172 House members including 9 Republicans, sat in a subcommittee and never got a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill rewrote the Clean Water Act's definition of 'fill material' so that waste—such as the rubble left by mountaintop removal coal mining—could no longer be dumped into streams and valleys under the easier 'fill' permit. Instead, any waste discharged into water would have to pass the much stricter pollution-discharge permitting process, which in practice stops dumping it as fill [S2][S3]. The bill never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near or downstream of streams and rivers that would otherwise receive mining waste—the bill would keep that waste out of waterways, protecting drinking water sources, fish, and the streams and rivers themselves [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near Appalachian streams and rivers

how_it_helps.text: Defines 'fill material' to exclude any pollutant discharged into water primarily to dispose of waste, so waste cannot be permitted as fill [S2][S3].
That pushes waste dumping onto the stricter pollution-discharge permitting track of the Clean Water Act instead of the Corps of Engineers' fill-permit track [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Coal companies that use mountaintop removal, whose cheapest way to dispose of rubble—pushing it into adjacent valleys and streams—would no longer be available as a permitted 'fill' activity [S2]. Some of that cost would flow into coal prices and mining employment in coal regions.

drawbacks.text: Restricting valley fills raises disposal costs for Appalachian coal operators and could cost mining jobs in coal-dependent communities, a real cost an honest supporter must weigh [S2].
A blanket statutory definition of fill material leaves less room for regulators to tailor permits case by case, which could also complicate other projects that place material in waters.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit—keeping industrial waste out of streams and rivers that supply drinking water and support aquatic life—is broad and lasting. The cost falls on a specific industry that had relied on the cheaper permitting route since the 2002 rule change, with some effect on coal jobs. On balance the protection is substantial and the cost is concentrated, though the loss of mining jobs in Appalachia is a genuine hardship that deserves attention.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its Water Resources subcommittee, where it sat until Congress ended—no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the bill on March 4, 2009 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the same day [S5].
Two days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, and no further action followed for the rest of the Congress [S5].
It drew 172 cosponsors—163 of 253 House Democrats and 9 of 178 House Republicans—far more than the 218 needed to pass the House [S1][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal operators using mountaintop removal kept the cheaper dumping route; no one who drinks from affected watersheds gained anything.

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to keep waste out of the Clean Water Act's fill-permit program [S1][S3].

for.name: 9 of 178 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it support from both parties [S1][S4].

against.name: James Oberstar
against.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee to which the bill was referred, never brought it to a markup or vote during the Congress.

against.name: Coal industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill, which would end the practice of dumping mining rubble into valleys and streams under fill permits.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship crossed party lines—163 of 253 Democrats and 9 of 178 Republicans—but the bill never reached the floor, so no roll-call vote shows how the chamber would have divided.

industries.note: The bill would end the industry's ability to dump mine rubble into streams and valleys under the easier fill-permit process, forcing it onto the stricter pollution-discharge track [S2]. Its interest ran against communities whose water those streams feed.

industries.industry: Construction and dredging firms that place fill in waters
industries.note: The statutory definition covers any material that replaces waters with dry land, but the exclusion applies to waste; ordinary fill projects would still be permitted. The bill mainly targeted waste dumping, not routine construction fills [S3].
